newsitem.title: USA: USDA asks Congress to help dairy farmers.
newsitem.headline: USDA asks Congress to help dairy farmers.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman urged Congress to consider an options pilot program for dairy farmers or some form of a modified price support program to help dairy producers struggling with low prices, according to a letter made public on Friday.

Glickman told Sen. Richard Lugar, head of the Senate's agriculture committee, and Rep. Bob Smith, head of the House agriculture committee, that the USDA has already purchased millions of pounds of dairy products for U.S. food programs to help prop up milk prices.

"While USDA will aggressively continue these efforts, I believe that the administration and the Congress must find additional tools to help dairy producers cope with the volatility in farm-level milk prices and effectively manage their operations in an increasingly market-oriented dairy policy regime," Glickman said in the letter, dated July 9.
Several dairy and farm groups have scheduled a demonstration at the USDA in Washington on July 15 to draw attention to sinking milk prices.

The federal dairy price support program is being phased out as part of last year's landmark farm bill and will end in 2000. After peaking at $13.48 per cwt in the early 1980s, the milk price support level is now at $10.20 per cwt.
In the letter, Glickman outlined four possible policies for congress to consider, saying that the USDA did not endorse any of them:
First, an options pilot program could help producers use risk management tools. Under the current law, such a program would have to be budget-neutral and funded by the USDA's Commodity Credit Corp.
"It is likely to be impossible to design a program under the 1996 Farm Bill that would result in more than negligible participation," the letter said.

A second option is to create a temporary price floor under federal milk marketing orders, Glickman said. Such a program would require a formal rulemaking procedure that would take at least six months, and would run contrary to the aims of last year's farm legislation.

A third option would be to redesign the price support program to help dairy farmers until risk management tools are available, he said. Such a program would increase government intervention in the dairy markets and would mean unbudgeted costs.

And a final option would be to launch a processor recourse loan program that would complement the current dairy purchase program. The program could operate at a price level about the current level of support of $10.20 per cwt, and repayment of loans could be required within the same fiscal year, Glickman said.
